idiom_name: Core Data managed object graph with cascade delete rules
implementation_notes: Core Data is the pattern's Swift home: the composite is an NSManagedObject whose relationships hold the dependents, the delete rule cascadeDeleteRule removes them when the root is deleted, and NSManagedObjectContext acts as the unit of work whose save() writes the whole graph. Because changes are tracked in the context, one save commits the cluster. The delete rule is schema metadata - changing it later needs a model version and migration, and the wrong rule destroys data on the next save.
pitfalls: deleteRule is not code: changing it after the store exists requires a new model version and migration, and a mis-set rule deletes dependents on the next save of the parent.
A context save writes every registered change, not just the cluster being edited; in large contexts that makes an innocuous save expensive and surprising.
NSManagedObject instances belong to their context's queue - moving them across queues, or between SwiftUI views and background contexts, causes the classic intermittent crashes.

variants.name: SwiftData @Model with @Relationship(.cascade)
variants.implementation_notes: SwiftData is Apple's macro-based successor: @Model turns the class into a persistent type, relationships are inferred from model-typed properties, and @Relationship(.cascade) replaces the Core Data delete rule while ModelContext.save() remains the unit of work. Choose it for new code where the schema lives in Swift source instead of an .xcdatamodeld file.
pitfalls: Relationships are inferred from the model graph: two types related through more than one property need the inverse declared explicitly, or the wrong pair is linked.
Deleting a related instance nullifies by default; without an explicit cascade rule the dependent object survives as an orphan.
